RECRUITING-CTX-G1.title: Candidate resume and open role packet (Teverbaugh, Senior Engineering Manager)
RECRUITING-CTX-G1.text:
CANDIDATE RESUME AND OPEN ROLE PACKET

PART 1 - CANDIDATE RESUME
Marisol Teverbaugh
Calder Falls, OR

Summary
Engineering leader with eleven years in backend and platform engineering. Currently manages a platform team of seven engineers at Ostrander Labs.

Experience
Ostrander Labs - Engineering Manager, Platform (Dec 2022 to present)
- Manage seven direct reports; run weekly one-on-ones and quarterly planning.
- Built the company's first on-call rotation and incident review process; production incidents down 41 percent over two years.
- Hired four engineers, two of whom have since been promoted to senior.
- Worked with finance on cloud cost reviews; monthly infrastructure spend down 22 percent.

Tallowick Payments - Tech Lead, Ledger Team (Sep 2021 to Nov 2022, 14 months)
- Led five engineers rebuilding the ledger reconciliation service in Go, Kafka and PostgreSQL.
- Daily batch reconciliation failures fell from 38 percent to 9 percent.
- Role ended when a reorganization closed the ledger product line.

Career break (Mar 2021 to Aug 2021)
- Full-time family caregiving.

Corvane Logistics Tech - Software Engineer, then Senior Software Engineer (Nov 2017 to Feb 2021)
- Promoted to Senior in January 2019.
- Led the migration of the route-dispatch service from a monolith into four services with a team of four engineers; p95 dispatch latency fell from 900 ms to 310 ms.
- Ran the on-call rotation for the dispatch services for two years.

Brindlemoor Software - Software Engineer (Jun 2015 to Oct 2017)
- Built customer-facing reporting features in Kotlin and PostgreSQL.

Education
BSc Computer Science, Ferncliff University, 2015

Skills
Go, Kotlin, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Kubernetes, incident management, hiring, budget planning

Application form answers
Current base salary: 148,000 USD
Target base salary: 165,000 to 175,000 USD
Notice period: six weeks
Earliest start: mid-November 2026
Reason for leaving current role, in her words: "Looking for a larger platform scope."

PART 2 - OPEN ROLE
Senior Engineering Manager, Platform - Quillfeather Systems
Location: Calder Falls, OR, hybrid with two office days per week
Base salary band: 160,000 to 185,000 USD plus annual bonus
Reports to: Halvard Ketterly, VP Engineering

The team
The Platform group has nine engineers and two contractors. It owns the internal deploy pipeline, the message bus, and the on-call tooling used by every product team. Two engineering roles on the team are currently open.

Responsibilities
- Lead and grow the Platform group, including hiring for the two open roles.
- Own the platform on-call rotation and post-incident reviews.
- Partner with finance on infrastructure budget.
- Set the quarterly roadmap with product engineering leads.

Requirements
- 8 or more years of software engineering experience.
- 3 or more years managing engineers.
- Hands-on background in distributed systems built on a message bus.
- Track record of hiring and developing engineers.
Nice to have: cloud cost management experience.

Hiring process
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), hiring manager conversation, technical deep dive with two staff engineers, panel interview, reference checks. The team hopes to have the role filled within eight weeks of the offer.

RECRUITING-CTX-C1.title: Resume with internal contradictions plus mismatched job description (Blackwell-Nakamura)
RECRUITING-CTX-C1.text:
RESUME - TEODOR BLACKWELL-NAKAMURA
Director of Engineering | Halden Bay, WA

Summary
Engineering director with 9 years of experience leading teams. Built and ran an engineering organization of 15 people. Hands-on with Java, Python and AWS. Known for turning around underperforming delivery teams.

Experience
Lattimer Dynamics - Senior Software Engineer (Jan 2019 to Dec 2022)
- Promoted to Engineering Lead in March 2021.
- Led a team of 5 engineers on the billing platform rewrite.
- Cut deployment time from 4 hours to 25 minutes.
- Represented engineering in quarterly planning with the finance group.

Vesperline Cloud - Director of Engineering (Mar 2022 to Dec 2023)
- Managed 8 engineers across two squads.
- Full-time role, fully remote.
- Owned the annual engineering budget of 2.1 million USD.
- Introduced a weekly architecture review that was adopted company-wide.

Orrin Systems - Software Engineer (Jun 2011 to Aug 2013)
- Built internal inventory tools in Java.

Career gap: none.

Education
BSc Computer Science, Marrow State University, graduated 2014

Skills
Java, Python, AWS, Terraform, team building, roadmap planning

Additional
Spoke at an internal engineering summit in 2022. Mentored junior engineers. Available to start with two weeks notice.

Reference note
Former manager at Lattimer Dynamics: "Teodor was a strong senior engineer who I would happily rehire in the same role."

JOB DESCRIPTION EXCERPT - Engineering Manager, Payments (Northfield Works)
Responsibilities: lead the payments engineering group, manage three engineering managers, and own the payments on-call program.
Requirements: 10 or more years of experience, including at least 5 years managing managers.
Location: fully remote. Office attendance three days per week.
Salary: 150,000 to 170,000 USD. Budget approved for candidates up to 140,000 USD.

RECRUITING-CTX-I1.title: Office snack and beverage budget memo
RECRUITING-CTX-I1.text:
MEMO: OFFICE SNACK AND BEVERAGE BUDGET, FOURTH QUARTER
To: All Floor 3 staff, Dunmore Building
From: Facilities coordination
Date: 3 October

Hello everyone,

After the survey last month, the facilities team has agreed the following changes to the shared kitchen budget for the fourth quarter.

The total quarterly snack and beverage budget stays at 1,800 USD. The new coffee machine on Floor 3 will be leased rather than purchased, which frees roughly 240 USD per quarter compared with last year. That amount moves to fresh fruit, which staff ranked first in the survey.

Changes:
- Fruit delivery moves from every other Monday to every Monday.
- Sparkling water is kept, but the flavored varieties are reduced from six to three.
- Individually wrapped chocolate is removed from the shared shelf. A small tin will remain at reception for visitors.
- Oat milk is added as the second milk option. Almond milk is discontinued.
- The Friday cake fund is capped at 60 USD per month and is now paid from team budgets, not from the shared kitchen budget.

Please label personal food in the fridge with your name and the date. Anything unlabeled after Friday afternoon will be cleared out.

Requests for additions should go to the facilities inbox by the 20th of each month. We review requests once a month and cannot promise every item will be added.

Thank you,
Facilities coordination

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: That break in 2021 was family stuff. I'd rather not go into it.
items.answer: That's a fair boundary, and the résumé already covers it as full-time family caregiving from March to August 2021, so you don't need to press. Move to what matters for the role: "Understood, I won't push on that. What I'd like to hear is how you got back up to speed when you returned, and what you were looking for in your next role."

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Why did that happen?
conversation: CANDIDATE: Quick update: the integration slipped by about two weeks. The vendor changed their API without telling us.
USER (spoken): Okay. That's not ideal.
CANDIDATE: Right. And the original date was already tight.
items.answer: Ask: "What's your understanding of why the vendor changed the API, and what did we have in place to catch a change like that before it hit us?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Honestly, I feel like I've hit a ceiling. Same title, same scope, four years.
items.answer: That's a real signal, so let's test whether it's the role or the company. Ask: "What have you tried to change that, and what did your manager say when you raised it?" Then follow with "If the scope here can't grow, what would you want your next role to look like?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: I owned the entire migration end to end, pretty much by myself.
items.answer: That's a big claim, so pin down the boundary: "End to end by yourself is a lot. Walk me through what you personally did versus what the team handled, and who else was involved." Then listen for whether they can name the parts they didn't own.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Compare his resume to the job requirements. List anything that doesn't add up, tell me what to ask him about, and say whether the problems look serious or just sloppy writing.
items.answer:
The dates overlap: Lattimer runs Jan 2019 to Dec 2022 while Vesperline runs Mar 2022 to Dec 2023, and the resume claims no career gap. Ask: "Walk me through your timeline from 2019 to 2023. Were Lattimer and Vesperline concurrent, and which was full-time?" Also probe the manager-of-managers requirement, since the resume shows 8 engineers across two squads, not three EMs.

The overlap looks like sloppy writing rather than fabrication, but the 5-years-managing-managers gap is real and serious for this role.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What's the biggest risk?
items.answer: The biggest risk I'd flag is that we move on a decision before the assumptions behind it are actually tested. I'd rather surface that early than discover it later.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Why's the position open?
conversation: CANDIDATE: Sorry, one second, my daughter is asking about her lunch.
USER (spoken): Of course.
CANDIDATE: Okay, sorry, all sorted.
items.answer: That's a fair question to turn back on them. Ask: "What's driving the hire on your side, is this a backfill or a new role, and what happened that made it urgent now?" Then listen for whether it's growth, a departure, or a restructure, since that shapes what they'll expect from whoever steps in.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What do you think?
items.answer: Ask: "What's your honest take on what we just went through? If you were in my seat, what would you be most concerned about, and what would you want to dig into next?" That gets you a judgment call and a self-directed follow-up instead of a recap.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: So how many people did she actually manage?
conversation: CANDIDATE: I ran a team of about ten engineers at my last company.
USER (spoken): Were they all direct reports?
CANDIDATE: Well, six reported to me directly, and four were dotted-line from other managers, plus a couple of contractors.
items.answer: I don't have a number for that. Ask her directly: "How many people reported to you, and did you own their reviews and hiring?" That pins down real scope versus informal mentoring.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: How big was the team?
conversation: USER (spoken): What was the biggest project at your last company?
CANDIDATE: The service migration. We moved the whole routing service off the old monolith and it went really well, everyone was thrilled.
USER (typed to Natively): What was your contribution?

NATIVELY: The candidate gave you a headline, not a contribution. Ask: "What was your specific role on that migration, and what part of it did you own end to end?" Then follow with "What broke or got hard along the way, and how did you handle it?" The "everyone was thrilled" line is a claim with no evidence behind it yet.
items.answer: The candidate hasn't given a team size, so don't let the number stand in for the contribution. Ask: "How big was the team on that migration, and how many people reported to you or worked directly on your part of it?" Then pin the ownership: "Of that group, which piece was yours alone to deliver?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Those last two years, from 2022 on, were honestly the best of my time there.
conversation: USER (spoken): When did you join Marlowe Freight?
CANDIDATE: I joined Marlowe Freight in 2019 and stayed about three years.
USER (spoken): And why did you leave?
CANDIDATE: The reorg. I left in early 2024, right after they merged two divisions.
items.answer: That's a nice note to build on. Ask: "What made those two years the best? Was it the work itself, the team, or something about the company at that stage?" Then follow with: "And what changed after the merger that made you decide to leave?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What can I ask to verify that without sounding like I doubt her, what proof could she reasonably show, and when would I need to go to references instead?
conversation: USER (spoken): What's the project you're proudest of?
CANDIDATE: Probably the payments rebuild at my last company. I led the whole thing and we cut the failure rate by a lot.
items.answer: She said "a lot" and "led the whole thing," so the probe is for the number and her specific role. Ask: "What was the failure rate before and after, and what part did you personally own versus the team?" If she can't produce a before-and-after figure or name her own decisions, that's when you go to references.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Give me a short scorecard for culture fit I can use across the panel.
items.answer:
A short scorecard the panel can fill in after each interview: rate 1 to 5 on each, then one line of evidence.

1. **Ownership**: do they describe what they personally decided and did, not just what the team shipped?
2. **Specificity**: concrete examples with real constraints, or general claims that could apply anywhere?
3. **Collaboration**: how they handled disagreement and credit, with a named example?
4. **Feedback**: do they seek it and act on it, and can they give it directly?
5. **Motivation**: why this role and this team, in their own words?

Keep the evidence line mandatory, so scores stay anchored to what was actually said rather than a gut feeling.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: It just wasn't the right fit, and I'd rather not get into it.
conversation: CANDIDATE (heard): I left that job after about a year.

NATIVELY: That's a short tenure, so get the reason without sounding like you're judging it. Ask: "What made you decide to move on at that point, and what were you hoping the next role would give you that this one didn't?" Then follow with "Was the decision yours, or was it mutual?" to pin down whether they left or were managed out.
items.answer: They've closed the door, so don't push on the reason. Ask instead: "That's fair, I won't press on it. What I do want to understand is what I'm looking for now, and what would make this role a better fit than that one." If they stay vague, one neutral follow-up: "Was leaving your call, or something the company decided?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: That doesn't sound right to me.
items.answer: Fair enough, let's pin down where we disagree. Which part doesn't sit right with you, the conclusion or the reasoning behind it? If you tell me the specific piece, I can walk you through exactly how I got there.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Who needs to know about this?
conversation: CANDIDATE: Quick update: the integration slipped by about two weeks. The vendor changed their API without telling us.
USER (spoken): Okay. That's not ideal.
CANDIDATE: Right. And the original date was already tight.
items.answer: The candidate hasn't answered anything yet, so there's no evidence to assess. Ask: "Who else needs to know about the slip, and what's your plan for telling them?" Then follow with "What's the new date, and what has to give to hit it?"
